title: Practice Set DM5 — Cleaning: Nulls, Duplicates, Whitespace
description: Recognition track capstone: cleaning pipelines. Order dependencies in dropna/fillna, then a 30-line Bronze→Silver pipeline to read line by line. Companion to the Foundations Cleaning chapter.

tasks.title: Cleaning Operations Have Order Dependencies

description.context: Pandas dropna() takes a `subset` parameter and a `how` parameter, and they interact in a way Junior engineers often misread. By default `how='any'` — meaning a row is dropped if ANY column in the subset is null. So passing subset=['meter_id', 'region'] does NOT mean 'drop rows missing meter_id, then handle region separately'; it means 'drop rows where meter_id OR region is null'. The opposite mode `how='all'` only drops rows where every subset column is null. To drop on a single column the subset must contain ONLY that column. This bug is invisible at runtime because no error is raised — the only symptom is fewer rows than expected reaching the next step.
description.task: Why does the result contain fewer 'UNKNOWN' regions than QA expected?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: 6-row Bronze sample. M-002 has missing meter_id (unrecoverable). M-003 and M-005 have missing region (recoverable — should become 'UNKNOWN'). M-006 has both missing (unrecoverable due to meter_id).

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
# Spec: drop rows where meter_id is missing, then fill missing region with 'UNKNOWN'.
step1 = df.dropna(subset=['meter_id', 'region'])
step2 = step1.fillna({'region': 'UNKNOWN'})
result = step2

fields.label: Why does the result contain fewer 'UNKNOWN' regions than QA expected?
options: fillna uses the wrong syntax — Pandas expects fillna(value='UNKNOWN', subset=['region']) not the dict form, so fillna runs on every column and the 'UNKNOWN' count gets diluted.

The dropna subset is too wide — with default how='any', subset=['meter_id','region'] drops a row if EITHER column is null, so the rows with only region missing are dropped here too and never reach fillna. Fix: subset=['meter_id'] only.

fillna's value 'UNKNOWN' is a Python string but region was silently cast to categorical earlier, so fillna fails on type mismatch and the missing-region rows end up as the string 'nan' instead of 'UNKNOWN'.
The pipeline assigns result = step2 but should assign result = df — a name-shadowing bug where step2 is computed correctly but the wrong variable reaches result, leaving original nulls intact.
fields.correctAnswer: The dropna subset is too wide — with default how='any', subset=['meter_id','region'] drops a row if EITHER column is null, so the rows with only region missing are dropped here too and never reach fillna. Fix: subset=['meter_id'] only.
fields.rationale: dropna defaults to how='any', meaning 'drop if ANY column in the subset is null'. Passing subset=['meter_id', 'region'] therefore drops both unrecoverable rows (missing meter_id) AND the recoverable ones (only region missing) — the latter group never reaches fillna. The fix is dropna(subset=['meter_id']) so only meter_id-missing rows are dropped, leaving region-missing rows for the fillna step. The most common Junior confusion is reading 'subset=[A, B]' as 'apply this stage to A separately, then to B' — but it is one combined predicate, OR'd by default.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Invents a wrong fillna signature. The dict form fillna({'region': 'UNKNOWN'}) is valid and common.

Option C: Fabricates a categorical cast not present in the snippet. region is a regular string column.

Option D: The assignment chain step1=..., step2=..., result=step2 is correct and free of shadowing — picking D is grasping at a generic suspicion.

tasks.title: The 30-Line Bronze-To-Silver Cleaning Pipeline

description.context: Cleaning pipelines mix two kinds of operations: VALUE changes (the cell contents are different after) and DTYPE changes (the column's storage type is different after). pd.to_datetime parses an ISO string into a datetime64 representation — same instant in time, different storage type. That is a pure dtype change. By contrast pd.to_numeric(..., errors='coerce') changes BOTH dtype (object to float64) AND values (anything unparseable becomes NaN). String methods like str.upper() and str.strip() change values but leave dtype untouched (object stays object). Telling the two apart is a key reading-comprehension skill for cleaning code reviews.
description.task: Which line is the only line that changes the dtype of a column rather than its values?

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
import pandas as pd
from pandas.api.types import is_numeric_dtype

# Line 1: read raw Bronze CSV (intentionally permissive — accepts mixed empty/null)
df = pd.read_csv('bronze/meters_2026-03-02.csv', keep_default_na=False, na_values=[''])

# Line 2: drop rows that are unrecoverable (no meter_id)
df = df.dropna(subset=['meter_id'])

# Line 3: standardize region casing — vendors send mixed case
df['region'] = df['region'].str.upper()

# Line 4: trim whitespace from string columns
for col in ['meter_id', 'region', 'customer_type', 'substation_id']:
    df[col] = df[col].str.strip()

# Line 5: parse the date column from string to datetime
df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['date'], format='%Y-%m-%d')

# Line 6: cast daily_kw to float, coercing parse failures to null
df['daily_kw'] = pd.to_numeric(df['daily_kw'], errors='coerce')

# Line 7: deduplicate exact duplicates (same meter, same date, same value)
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=['meter_id', 'date', 'daily_kw'])

# Line 8: fill missing region with the literal 'UNKNOWN' (recoverable downstream)
df['region'] = df['region'].fillna('UNKNOWN')

# Line 9: keep only the columns Silver needs
df = df[['meter_id', 'daily_kw', 'date', 'region', 'customer_type', 'substation_id']]

# Line 10: write Silver in Parquet with snappy compression
df.to_parquet('silver/meters_2026-03-02.parquet', compression='snappy', index=False)

fields.label: Which line is the only line that changes the dtype of a column rather than its values?
options: Line 3 (str.upper()) — uppercasing produces a new string array that Pandas tags with a refreshed dtype, so this is a dtype-only change even though the textual content is reinterpreted.
Line 6 (pd.to_numeric(errors='coerce')) — the cast from string to numeric is the only true dtype change; the other lines stay within object dtype and only modify values.
Line 4 (str.strip()) — whitespace trimming is the canonical Pandas dtype refresh on string columns; values stay the same, only the dtype is reset.

Line 5 (pd.to_datetime) — this is the only line whose primary effect is dtype (object to datetime64) without changing the underlying instants. Line 6 changes dtype too but ALSO changes values via errors='coerce'.
fields.correctAnswer: Line 5 (pd.to_datetime) — this is the only line whose primary effect is dtype (object to datetime64) without changing the underlying instants. Line 6 changes dtype too but ALSO changes values via errors='coerce'.
fields.rationale: Line 5 is the cleanest dtype-only change. The string '2026-03-01' and the datetime64 representation of March 1, 2026 are the SAME instant — only the storage type changes. Line 6 (pd.to_numeric with errors='coerce') does change dtype but it ALSO changes values: any unparseable string becomes NaN. The most common Junior confusion is treating 'cast' lines as a single category — but coerce-on-error makes line 6 a hybrid (type change + value change), while line 5 is pure type change.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Believes str.upper() refreshes dtype. It does not — output stays object dtype.

Option B: Half-right — line 6 IS a dtype change, but the question asks for the ONLY-dtype line; line 6 also mutates values via coerce.

Option C: Invents a 'dtype refresh on strip'. str.strip changes values; dtype is unchanged.
